bill.title: Carson City Public Land Correction Act
bill.latestActionText: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 488.

classification.plainSummary: This bill would correct land ownership boundaries in Carson City, Nevada. It appears to involve transferring or adjusting federal public land parcels, possibly to resolve mapping errors or align ownership with actual use. The bill's subject terms mention land transfers, geography and mapping, roads, utilities, and wildlife habitat, but without the bill text or a more detailed summary, the specific parcels and purposes cannot be described with certainty.

industries.rationale: The bill's subject terms include public utilities, suggesting it may affect utility infrastructure or rights-of-way on the land parcels being corrected.
Land transfers and boundary corrections in Carson City could affect property development, ownership rights, or land values in the area.

plain.whatItDoes: No one has written a summary of this bill yet. All we have is its title, and a title is not a description of a law. To find out what it does, you have to open the bill itself.
plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who drives. People who live near or work on federal land.
plain.everydayEffect: Nothing has changed yet. The title alone does not say what would change for you, and this tool will not guess. Most bills never become law.
plain.source: From the bill title, and from the subject labels that library staff put on it. There is no official summary of this bill yet.

method.formula: score = Σ_industries ( donorShare(industry) × billWeight(industry) ), where billWeight = classifierConfidence / Σ classifierConfidence. Range 0–1, read as a weighted share of disclosed itemized money.

ordinary.text: They wrote this bill. Sponsoring a bill about your own district's industry is the ordinary case, not the odd one.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
